title: Documentary Form Lab: The Same Story, Different Film
courseContext: DOC 515 — Foundations of Documentary Filmmaking · Module 1 · Lesson 2
privacy: Your responses stay in this browser. This lab has no login, backend, analytics, numerical score, or automatic Canvas submission.

introduction.heading: The Same Story, Different Film
introduction.lead: A documentary is never only its subject. Form is the creative agreement between filmmaker, contributor, and viewer.
paragraphs: In this lab, you will rebuild one filmable story through six contrasting documentary approaches.
The goal is not to discover a single correct form. It is to notice how each set of choices changes authority, emotion, evidence, ethics, filmmaker presence, and the scenes you are likely to pursue.
You will then test two forms against your own short-documentary idea and choose a provisional direction.
steps: Learn six concise, overlapping form definitions.
Inspect the people, place, labor, records, uncertainty, time, images, and sounds available in one community-garden story.
Draft six possible treatments from the same story material.
Compare two treatments side by side.
Apply two forms to your own project and export a provisional-form statement.
introduction.disclosure: The community-garden images are fictional teaching visuals. They do not depict real documentary contributors or events.

formsIntro.heading: Use forms as lenses, not rigid boxes
formsIntro.lead: Most documentaries are hybrids. Name the dominant logic, then notice what each borrowed form adds.
formsIntro.hybridNote: Hybrid is not an escape hatch. It is a pattern of deliberate borrowing.

forms.title: Observational
forms.definition: Stay close to unfolding behavior and let action carry meaning.
lookFor: Meaning built through selection and juxtaposition
forms.question: What can happen without being arranged?

model.treatment: Spend the final open weekend with the gardeners as they work, wait, disagree, and prepare to leave.
model.camera: Present for sustained action; little explanation in the moment.
model.pressure: The approaching closure reorganizes ordinary behavior.

forms.title: Issue-led / expository
forms.definition: Organize evidence and argument so the audience can follow a claim.
lookFor: Evidence arranged for clarity and consequence
forms.question: What must the audience understand—and why now?

model.treatment: Use the garden’s possible closure to investigate who controls neighborhood land—and who benefits.
model.camera: Gather interviews, public records, meetings, maps, and observable consequences.
model.pressure: Competing claims about value, ownership, and public good.

forms.title: Participatory
forms.definition: Let the encounter between filmmaker and contributor become part of the film.
forms.question: What does the encounter reveal?

model.treatment: The filmmaker joins the effort to save the garden and records how participation changes access and understanding.
model.camera: Questions, collaboration, and the filmmaker’s decisions remain audible or visible.
model.pressure: Can the filmmaker participate without disguising influence or making false promises?

forms.title: Reflexive
forms.definition: Make the process, construction, or uncertainty of documentary visible.
lookFor: The making of the film enters the film
Gaps, limits, or contradictions remain visible
forms.question: How is this account being made—and where does it fail?

model.treatment: Build the film around contradictory accounts—and the missing documents needed to know why the garden may close.
model.camera: Show searches, refusals, gaps, edits, and the limits of what can be verified.
model.pressure: The attempt to tell the story becomes evidence about power and knowledge.

forms.title: Poetic
forms.definition: Build meaning through rhythm, association, image, and sound.
lookFor: Sound and image carry ideas beyond explanation
forms.question: What can be felt before it is explained?

model.treatment: Compose a sensory elegy from soil, hands, voices, seasons, empty beds, and the sounds of surrounding construction.
model.camera: Collect image and sound motifs; build rhythm, association, and contrast.
model.pressure: Loss is felt through what changes in the place and its soundscape.

forms.title: Performative / personal
forms.definition: Use lived experience and embodied point of view as a way of knowing.
lookFor: The maker’s experience shapes the inquiry
forms.question: Why is this story being told from here, by this person?

model.treatment: A gardener tells the history of the place through the plants, objects, and memories that shaped her own life.
model.camera: First-person narration, embodied action, family archive, and intimate encounter.
model.pressure: The possible closure challenges identity, memory, and belonging.

storyWorld.heading: One story. Six possible films.
storyWorld.title: The community garden may close.
storyWorld.summary: The available story world contains people, place, labor, records, uncertainty, and time. The garden and closure threat remain; the form changes what counts as evidence, how the filmmaker is present, how camera and sound behave, and how authority and feeling are structured.
storyWorld.alt: A fictional older gardener holding seedlings in a city community garden while another person works in the background.
storyWorld.contactSheetAlt: Six fictional teaching views of a community garden: gardening labor, seedlings, a filmmaker recording, a notice on a fence, empty beds, and a seated gardener.

items.text: An effort to save the garden

builder.heading: Build six treatments from one story
builder.lead: Draft every version before comparing two. Select story material, order it into a possible progression, and state the choices each form asks you to make.
builder.emptyTray: No story material selected yet. Use Add to Treatment, then reorder with the buttons or drag items.

fields.label: Likely scene strategy
fields.prompt: What would the camera stay with, and what could develop?

fields.label: Filmmaker presence
fields.prompt: How visible or audible is the filmmaker, and how does that presence affect events?

fields.label: Evidence
fields.prompt: What will count as evidence in this version?

fields.label: Image and sound
fields.prompt: How will image and sound carry meaning?

fields.label: Ethical pressure
fields.prompt: What relationship, promise, limit, or risk needs attention?

builder.teacherNote: Model combinations are examples, not answers. Ask what each version makes possible, what it leaves out, and whether the filmmaker’s promises match the form.

comparison.heading: Compare two treatments side by side
comparison.lead: The garden, closure threat, people, place, access, and ethical obligations stay. The form changes the film’s consequences.

prompts.label: Authority
prompts.text: Who seems able to explain, interpret, or challenge the story in each version?

prompts.label: Emotion
prompts.text: How might each version shape what the audience feels—and when?

prompts.label: Ethics
prompts.text: What relationship, promise, omission, or distortion becomes more likely in each version?

prompts.label: Filmmaker presence
prompts.text: Where is the filmmaker positioned, and how does that position affect what can be known?

prompts.label: Likely scenes
prompts.text: Which scenes would each version pursue, and what might it fail to film?

ownProject.heading: Test two forms against your own documentary
ownProject.lead: Choose provisionally, not permanently. Your formal choice should respond to the story you can actually access and film.

fields.label: Specific story
fields.prompt: What unfolds, for whom, in what situation?

fields.label: Access and filmable situation
fields.prompt: Who, what, and where can you genuinely access? What can the camera encounter?

formPrompts.label: What could the first form reveal?
What might the first form risk hiding or distorting?
What could the second form contribute, reveal, or protect?
What small access or scene test will help you decide?

reflection.heading: Make a provisional form statement
reflection.lead: Form is a decision about how to meet reality. Name what the choice reveals and what it risks hiding.

prompts.label: Why does this form currently serve the story you can access and film?
What could a second form contribute?
What might the provisional form risk hiding?

teacherSupport.heading: Teacher Notes
teacherSupport.intro: Use these prompts to open discussion. Do not present a model treatment as the single correct creative answer.
questions: What does this form ask the camera to wait for?
What becomes authoritative, and whose knowledge becomes secondary?
How does filmmaker presence change access, responsibility, or trust?
What material is emphasized, and what could disappear from the account?
Which borrowed form would complicate the dominant logic productively?
